Patient Vignette: Mr. L. (Age 44, South East Asian, Married, Nurse)

Mr. L. is a 44-year-old married man of South East Asian descent who works as a registered nurse on a busy medical-surgical floor. He presents with a haunted, watchful quality, his eyes scanning the room as he speaks. He describes himself as having been a "fixer" his whole life—the person who calms a crashing patient, who soothes a frantic family. That sense of control was shattered eight months ago.

The event occurred on a Tuesday evening after a double shift. Mr. L. was walking the three blocks from the hospital to the commuter train station, a route he had taken for seven years. He was tired, thinking about a patient who had coded that afternoon. He did not see the two men until they were directly in front of him. One held a knife. They demanded his bag, his phone, his wallet. He remembers the cold metal of the blade pressing against his throat, the smell of stale cigarettes and sweat on the man’s jacket, the sound of his own breath catching. He complied immediately. He gave them everything. They ran. He stood there, on the sidewalk, for what felt like an hour but was probably two minutes, before a woman from a nearby café came out and asked if he was okay.

In the weeks that followed, Mr. L. tried to return to his normal life. He told his wife, "It was just a robbery. I didn't get hurt. It's fine." But he was not fine. The first thing to change was his walk home. He cannot do it. He now takes a rideshare from the hospital entrance directly to his garage, even though it costs him a significant portion of his paycheck. He feels a physical revulsion, a tightness in his chest, just looking at that block.

At work, his hands have begun to shake. He is a surgical nurse, known for his steady hands during suture assists. Now, when he is removing a central line or starting an IV, he sees the knife in his mind’s eye. The image overlays the patient’s skin. He has had to step out of two sterile procedures, claiming a sudden migraine. His colleagues, who once saw him as unflappable, now find him irritable and withdrawn. He snaps at the nursing assistants for small things, like a misplaced chart.

The hypervigilance is constant. In the break room, he sits with his back to the wall, facing the door. He cannot eat in the cafeteria because the noise and the movement of people feel like an assault. He has started scanning every person who enters a patient’s room, assessing them for threat. Last week, he nearly called security on a delivery man who was wearing a hooded sweatshirt, the same color as the man who held the knife.

His sleep is destroyed. He has nightmares, not of the robbery itself, but of being unable to move, of being trapped in a white, sterile room while a shadow approaches. He wakes up drenched in sweat, his heart pounding, convinced he is back on that sidewalk. His wife, a primary school teacher, has started sleeping in the guest room because his thrashing and crying out frighten her. He feels a deep, cold shame about this. He is supposed to be the caretaker, the strong one.

The worst part, he says, is the emotional numbness. He used to cry easily at a patient’s story or feel a deep satisfaction when a difficult case went well. Now, he feels hollow. When a patient on his floor died last week—a young woman he had grown fond of—he felt nothing. He went through the motions of the post-mortem care, his hands moving automatically, his mind a blank. He was terrified by his own lack of feeling. He thinks, "I used to care. What is wrong with me?"

He has not told anyone at work the full story. He is afraid they will think he is weak, that he cannot handle the stress of the job. He avoids the hospital’s security office. He avoids the street where it happened. He has started driving to work in a loop that adds twenty minutes to his commute, just to avoid the intersection where the woman from the café helped him. He feels as though his life has been reduced to a series of avoidances, a shrinking map of what he can tolerate. He sits in my office, a man who once held the hands of the dying, now unable to walk three blocks in the city he has lived in for twenty years.
